title: What money supply and monetary policy mean

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define money supply, define monetary policy, and state which institution carries it out.

blocks.heading: Money supply and the policy built on it
blocks.text: Money supply is the total stock of money in an economy at a point in time: the notes and coins in circulation plus the bank deposits that can be spent by card, cheque or transfer. Deposits count because they pay for goods in the same way cash does. Monetary policy is the use of changes in interest rates, the money supply and the foreign exchange rate to influence the economy's performance. In Namibia the Bank of Namibia, the central bank, carries it out, setting the rate at which it lends to commercial banks, and that rate shapes the loan and deposit rates banks offer households and firms. Central banks are often confused with commercial banks: a commercial bank takes deposits and makes loans, while the central bank stands above the banks and steers them. The Bank of Japan plays this steering role, as does the central bank of the Netherlands within the European system.
blocks.repair_note: Review fix: monetary policy measures now include the foreign exchange rate (claims 002, 004, 006 revised); leaked register wording removed from P01; authoring labels removed; flashcard answers trimmed for recall.

blocks.heading: One rate rise traced through a bank
blocks.text: In 2024 Oshakati Savings Bank charges households 6% a year on loans. The Bank of Namibia raises the rate at which it lends to commercial banks, so the commercial bank is likely to raise its loan rate to 9%, because its own funds cost more. The interest on a N$20 000 loan at 6% is 0.06 x N$20 000 = N$1 200 a year. At 9% it is 0.09 x N$20 000 = N$1 800. The gap of N$1 800 - N$1 200 = N$600 is what a borrowing household feels, so households tend to borrow less and the stock of money grows more slowly. This is the lever monetary policy pulls.
